output.title: Why transcript accuracy is not the whole question
output.body:
If you run a 1–10-person business, the real question is not whether a transcript is perfect. It is what happens after the transcript exists, and who is responsible for the next step.

That matters because a transcript only becomes useful when it helps someone act. In a customer call, that might mean a refund request is flagged, a technical issue is routed, or a follow-up commitment lands with the right person. If the transcript is just saved in a folder and read again by hand, you have improved the text, not the workflow. Helpful, but not the same thing.

The practical boundary is human approval. For money movement and other high-risk decisions, a person still has to review before anything irreversible happens. So “accurate enough” does not mean perfect in the abstract. It means accurate enough to reach the right reviewer with the right context.

The simplest diagnostic question is this: what happens to this transcript after it is generated? If the answer is “nothing,” transcript accuracy is not the bottleneck. If the answer is “it feeds a decision or another system,” then accuracy, routing, and human check-in are the workflow to design.

That is usually where small businesses stop debating the transcript and start looking at the process.
